title: Passive Pauli Toggling of Polarization Qubits in Optical Fibers: Error Bounds and QKD Performance
abstract: Polarization qubits offer a direct route to fiber-based quantum communication, yet the fiber that carries them also scrambles their reference frame through uncontrolled birefringence. Active compensation commonly relies on monitoring and feedback, raising a natural question: can the link itself suppress coherent polarization drift before it reaches the receiver? We show that it can within a regime of sufficiently correlated unitary drift. Our central idea is to embed a fixed cyclic sequence of Pauli rotations along the fiber, turning propagation distance into a spatial toggling frame. Rather than estimating and inverting the unknown transformation, the sequence repeatedly reverses its leading action. We establish exact refocusing for constant generators compatible with a two-segment echo, show that a four-frame Pauli cell cancels the leading contribution of any traceless quasi-static generator, and bound the residual error for smoothly varying birefringence. We then connect these guarantees to operational BB84 quantities, including measured QBERs, the resulting secret fraction, and insertion loss. In simulations of a 50 km fiber with spatially correlated birefringence, a representative design reduces the mean QBER from 6.11% to 0.224% at a device spacing of 1.25 km. With an assumed per-device transmission of t = 0.997, this raises the asymptotic key rate per launched pulse by a factor of approximately 2.5. For this parameter set, the best design in the tested scan is not the densest one: error suppression and optical loss create a finite operating window. These results provide a loss-aware design principle for passive polarization stabilization and suggest a low-overhead complement to active tracking in polarization-encoded QKD networks.
summary: This paper introduces a technique called passive Pauli toggling, where fixed Pauli rotations are embedded within an optical fiber to counteract polarization drift caused by birefringence. By repeatedly reversing the accumulated phase rotation, the scheme significantly reduces the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) and boosts the key rate for QKD systems. It offers a loss-aware design principle for stabilizing polarization qubits without requiring continuous active monitoring.
main_problem: To determine if the quantum channel itself (the optical fiber) can suppress coherent polarization drift in polarization qubits before active feedback is applied, thereby improving Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) performance.
main_result: The proposed passive Pauli toggling scheme significantly reduces the mean QBER (e.g., from 6.11% to 0.224% in simulation) and increases the asymptotic key rate by a factor of approximately 2.5.
method: The authors developed a spatial-control framework by embedding a fixed cyclic sequence of Pauli rotations along the fiber to repeatedly reverse the leading action of the accumulated polarization drift.
model_or_system: The system uses single-photon polarization qubits transmitted through an optical fiber, modeled by a spatial Schrödinger equation whose evolution is controlled by inserting ideal Pauli rotators at discrete segments.
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rates (QBERs) in the X and Z bases, the resulting secret fraction, and the asymptotic key rate per launched pulse.
important_parameters: The optimal design is constrained by a finite operating window determined by the balance between error suppression and optical loss.
main_assumptions: The model excludes polarization-dependent loss and Polarization-Mode Dispersion (PMD); the analysis assumes the Pauli-twirled description is an operational reduction for QBERs.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention a practical workflow table summarizing the measurement of error suppression, insertion penalty, and operational gain by scanning cell spacing.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for Pauli toggling, derives end-to-end residual-error bounds for noncommuting drift, connects these bounds to operational QKD quantities (QBERs), and concludes with a loss-aware design principle.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel, passive, and mathematically rigorous method to precondition quantum communication channels, shifting the burden of error correction from active feedback to the physical structure of the link itself.

Fig. 4 summarizes the engineering message. There is a finite design window, not a monotone rule that “more devices are always better.” For high-transmission devices, decreasing ℓinitially improves the rate because it suppresses coherent polarization errors. Once the QBER is already small, further densification only multiplies loss and reduces the launched-pulse key rate. This behavior is consistent with Eq.
